title: Pointers and the Memory Model
description: Addresses, dereferencing, and why C is so close to the metal

concepts.title: What a Pointer Actually Is
concepts.contentHtml:
A pointer in C is a variable that holds a memory address. int *p declares a pointer to an int; p = &x takes the address of x; *p dereferences — reading or writing the int at that address. That's it. Pointers are just numbers indexing into memory.

This explicit access to memory is C's defining feature. Where higher-level languages hide pointers behind references and garbage collection, C exposes them directly. You can do pointer arithmetic (p + 1 moves to the next int), cast between pointer types, take the address of any variable, and store pointers in data structures.

The cost: the compiler can't protect you. Dereferencing an invalid pointer (NULL, freed memory, out-of-bounds) corrupts memory or crashes. C trusts you completely. This is why C remains essential for systems programming (kernels, drivers, embedded, runtimes) and why it's been the source of decades of memory-safety bugs.

concepts.title: Stack vs Heap Allocation
concepts.contentHtml:
C distinguishes two main memory regions. The stack grows and shrinks with function calls — local variables live there, allocated on entry, freed on return. Stack allocation is just a register decrement; basically free. But stack values can't outlive their function: returning &localVar creates a dangling pointer, the canonical undefined-behavior bug.

The heap is for dynamic allocation. Call malloc(size) to request bytes; you get back a pointer that's valid until you call free(ptr). Heap memory persists across function calls but you must explicitly manage its lifetime. Forget to free → memory leak. Free twice → double-free corruption. Use after free → exploitable bug. Free a pointer you didn't malloc → crash.

The third region is static/global memory — variables declared static or at file scope. Allocated once at program start, freed at exit. No lifetime questions, but no per-call state either. C programmers must consciously choose where each value lives.

concepts.title: Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays
concepts.contentHtml:
In C, an array decays to a pointer when used in most expressions. int arr[10]; int *p = arr; is valid — arr evaluates to a pointer to its first element. arr[i] is exactly equivalent to *(arr + i). There's no separate "array type" at runtime; just a pointer and a (compile-time) length.

Pointer arithmetic respects type sizes. p + 1 on an int* moves 4 bytes (typical int size); on a char* it moves 1 byte. p2 - p1 returns the number of elements between them, not bytes. This makes it natural to walk through arrays element by element.

The danger: no bounds checking. arr[100] on a 10-element array is undefined behavior — usually you read or write whatever happens to be at that memory address. Buffer overflows are precisely this: writing past the end of an array, often onto the stack where return addresses live. Decades of security exploits have lived in this gap.

title: Manual Memory Management
description: malloc, free, and the bugs they enable

concepts.title: malloc, calloc, realloc, free
concepts.contentHtml:
The C standard library provides four heap-management functions. malloc(size) returns a pointer to size bytes of uninitialized memory (or NULL on failure). calloc(n, size) allocates zeroed memory for n elements. realloc(ptr, new_size) resizes an existing allocation, possibly moving it. free(ptr) releases memory back to the system.

Always check malloc's return: if (!p) { handle_oom(); }. Skipping this check means dereferencing NULL on memory exhaustion, crashing your program. Production C code checks every allocation.

Always pair allocations with frees. The standard pattern: every successful path to creating an object also has a path to destroying it. Common idioms: errors free and return early; functions that return ownership document it; functions that borrow promise not to free. C has no syntax to enforce these contracts — they live in comments and convention.

concepts.title: The Classic Memory Bugs
concepts.contentHtml:
Manual memory management opens up famous categories of bugs.

Memory leak: forget to free, memory grows forever. In long-running services, leaks crash production. Tools like Valgrind and AddressSanitizer (ASan) detect them. Use-after-free: free a pointer, then read or write through it. The memory may have been reallocated; you're stomping on something else. Highly exploitable.

Double free: call free twice on the same pointer. Heap metadata corrupts, often crashing later or letting attackers control allocations. Buffer overflow: write past the end of an array. Smashes the stack frame, overwriting return addresses or function pointers. This was the classic 1990s exploit; modern mitigations (ASLR, DEP, stack canaries) make it harder but not impossible.

The unifying lesson: C requires discipline. Every memory bug is silent until it triggers. Modern C developers use ASan (compile with -fsanitize=address), valgrind, static analyzers, fuzz testing, and code review to find these before production.
mathExpressions: \text{leak, UAF, double free, overflow} \quad \text{(all silent until exploited)}

concepts.title: Ownership Conventions and RAII (in C)
concepts.contentHtml:
C has no destructors. The compiler can't run cleanup code when a variable leaves scope. So C programmers establish ownership conventions: who's responsible for freeing each allocation?

Common patterns: creator owns (the function that allocates also frees, or hands ownership to a caller documented as such). Borrowed pointers (function uses a pointer but doesn't free — caller retains ownership). Containers own elements (a list owns its nodes; freeing the list also frees each node).

Some C codebases simulate RAII using cleanup attributes (GCC's __attribute__((cleanup)), also via defer in modern C25). The Linux kernel uses kfree + carefully named lifetimes; FFmpeg uses ref-counting on certain objects; OpenSSL has explicit init/free pairs. Without a borrow checker, every C codebase reinvents these conventions and pays vigilance tax forever. This is the gap Rust exists to close.
mathExpressions: \text{ownership: who frees this?} \quad \text{(by convention, not by language)}

title: Strings, Arrays, and Structs
description: C's lean data types and their many footguns

concepts.title: C Strings: Just Null-Terminated char Arrays
concepts.contentHtml:
C has no string type. A C string is just an array of char ending in '\0' (the null terminator). Standard library functions (strlen, strcpy, printf) walk the array until they find the terminator.

This design has serious downsides. strlen is O(n) — must scan to find the end. strcpy has no length parameter and writes until it hits a terminator, easily overrunning the destination buffer. The strn- variants (strncpy, strncat) take lengths but have their own subtle bugs (strncpy may not null-terminate the result).

Modern C code uses safer alternatives: snprintf for formatted strings, careful length tracking, often custom string types. Some codebases adopt length-prefixed strings (length + buffer) to avoid the terminator entirely. The key safety habit: always know the maximum size you can write; never trust input lengths from outside.
mathExpressions: \text{C string: } [c_0, c_1, \ldots, c_{n-1}, \backslash 0] \quad \text{strlen} = n, \text{ no length stored}

concepts.title: Structs and Memory Layout
concepts.contentHtml:
A struct groups multiple values into one type: struct Point { int x; int y; };. Structs are stored contiguously in memory; you can take pointers to them, pass by value (copies the whole struct), or pass by pointer (shares the same one).

The catch is padding. Compilers may insert unused bytes between struct members to satisfy alignment requirements. struct { char c; int i; } typically takes 8 bytes (1 + 3 padding + 4), not 5. Reordering members from largest to smallest minimizes padding. Performance-critical or wire-format code uses __attribute__((packed)) to disable padding (with portability and speed costs).

Structs are the foundation of C's data modeling. Linked lists, trees, hash tables — all are structs with pointer fields. Without classes or methods, the design pattern is: struct for state, free functions taking a pointer to the struct as their first parameter. The Linux kernel and most C libraries follow this pattern systematically.

concepts.title: Function Pointers and Generic Code
concepts.contentHtml:
C lets you store function addresses in pointers: int (*compare)(const void *, const void *). The standard qsort uses this for generic sorting — pass it an array, an element size, and a comparison function pointer.

Function pointers enable many patterns: callbacks (event handlers, signal handlers), dispatch tables (interpreters, jump tables), plugin systems (loaded with dlopen, address resolved with dlsym), vtables for OOP-in-C (Linux kernel structs with function-pointer fields).

For generic code, C uses void * (untyped pointers) plus explicit size info. qsort(arr, n, sizeof(*arr), cmp) works on any type because it manipulates raw bytes via the size and comparator. Tradeoff: zero compile-time type checks. C++ templates and Rust generics evolved as type-safe alternatives, but the void-pointer trick is everywhere in idiomatic C.

title: Undefined Behavior
description: The compiler's right to do anything when you break the rules

concepts.title: What Undefined Behavior Means
concepts.contentHtml:
The C standard defines a set of rules programs must follow. Violating any rule is undefined behavior (UB): the compiler is allowed to do literally anything. Crash, return wrong values, format your hard drive (theoretically), travel back in time. The standard provides no guarantees.

Common UBs: signed integer overflow, out-of-bounds array access, dereferencing NULL or freed pointers, reading uninitialized memory, breaking strict aliasing rules, modifying a variable twice between sequence points (i = i++), shift past the type width.

The shocking part: modern compilers actively exploit UB for optimization. If your code performs UB, the compiler assumes you didn't (because you promised to follow the rules) and may delete the code path entirely. if (x + 1 < x) panic(); looks like an overflow check, but on a signed int, the compiler knows signed overflow is UB, so it deletes the panic call. This is real and surprising; many CVEs trace back to UB-based optimizer behavior.
mathExpressions: \text{UB: standard says nothing} \implies \text{compiler may do anything}

concepts.title: The Strict Aliasing Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
The strict aliasing rule says you can't access an object through a pointer of an incompatible type (with a few exceptions). float f = 1.5; uint32_t bits = *(uint32_t*)&f; looks like a reasonable bit reinterpretation but is undefined behavior — accessing a float through a uint32_t pointer.

The compiler uses this rule for optimization: it assumes pointers of different types don't alias, so it can reorder reads and writes between them. Code that violates strict aliasing may work for years, then break with a new compiler version or optimization level.

The correct way to bit-reinterpret: use memcpy: memcpy(&bits, &f, sizeof(bits));. The compiler optimizes memcpy of a known size into a single load/store, with no UB. Or use a union (well-defined on most compilers, technically UB pre-C99). Or std::bit_cast in C++20. Modern systems code does this constantly; doing it correctly is mandatory.
mathExpressions: \text{type T pointer cannot alias type U pointer} \implies \text{compiler reorders freely}

concepts.title: Sanitizers, Static Analysis, and Defensive Coding
concepts.contentHtml:
The defense against UB is rigorous tooling. AddressSanitizer (ASan) catches use-after-free, buffer overflows, and many heap bugs at runtime — compile with -fsanitize=address. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) catches signed overflow, null deref, alignment violations. ThreadSanitizer (TSan) catches data races. MemorySanitizer (MSan) finds reads of uninitialized memory.

Static analyzers (clang-tidy, cppcheck, Coverity, PVS-Studio) catch many bugs at compile time without running the code. Compilers themselves warn about many issues with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror. Fuzzers (libFuzzer, AFL++, OSS-Fuzz) feed random inputs into your code looking for crashes — Google's OSS-Fuzz has found tens of thousands of bugs in major open-source C projects.

Modern C development is unimaginable without these tools. Production-quality C requires running the test suite under all sanitizers in CI, fuzzing the parser surfaces, and treating warnings as errors. The language hasn't gotten safer, but the tooling has.

title: The Standard Library and Tooling
description: libc, build systems, and where C still wins

concepts.title: The C Standard Library
concepts.contentHtml:
C's standard library is small and remarkably stable. stdio.h: I/O (printf, scanf, fopen). stdlib.h: memory, conversions, exit. string.h: string manipulation. math.h: floating point. time.h: clock and date functions. stdint.h: fixed-size integers (uint32_t). assert.h: debugging assertions.

Compared to other languages, libc is tiny. There are no containers (no list, no hashmap), no networking, no JSON parsing, no regex (well, regex.h is POSIX but not C standard), no thread synchronization until C11. The philosophy: provide primitives, let third-party libraries fill the rest.

For practical work, you reach for system libraries (POSIX functions like sockets, mmap, pthreads), libraries from your platform (Win32, libdispatch on macOS), or community projects (zlib, libcurl, OpenSSL, SDL, GTK). C is the universal interface — almost every other language can call C functions, which is why C ABIs are the lingua franca of cross-language interop.
mathExpressions: \text{libc: small primitives} \quad \text{POSIX/system libs: rest of the OS}

concepts.title: Compiling and Linking
concepts.contentHtml:
The C build process has clear stages. Preprocessor: handles #include, #define, #ifdef. Compiler: turns each .c file into an object file (.o). Linker: combines object files and libraries into the final executable.

Each step has its own tooling. cpp for preprocessing, cc1 or clang for compilation, ld for linking. Most of the time you invoke them all together via gcc or clang. Build systems orchestrate this for large projects: Make (the original), CMake (cross-platform meta-build), Meson + Ninja (modern, fast), Bazel (Google-scale).

The classic pain point: header files. Every file that uses a function needs to include its declaration. Forward declarations, include guards (#ifndef...#define...#endif), #pragma once, transitive include chains, and recompilation cascades all stem from this design. C++20's modules aim to fix this; C is still working on it.

concepts.title: Where C Still Wins, and What's Replacing It
concepts.contentHtml:
C remains the language of choice in domains where memory layout, performance, and tight resource control matter most: operating system kernels (Linux, FreeBSD), embedded systems (firmware, microcontrollers), language runtimes (CPython, V8, JVM are partly C/C++), databases (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis), cryptography libraries (OpenSSL, libsodium), and video codecs.

The reasons: ABI stability (libc has been compatible since the 1980s), tiny runtime, every platform has a C compiler, predictable performance, and the ability to interop with everything. When a new language wants to be "systems-level," being able to call into and be called from C is mandatory.

The challengers are real. Rust offers memory safety without GC and is being adopted in the Linux kernel, Firefox, Cloudflare. Zig offers C's spirit with better ergonomics. C++ has long offered higher-level abstractions on the C foundation. But C itself isn't going anywhere — its installed base, ecosystem, and ABI lock-in are too deep. Knowing C is still the foundational systems-programming skill.
mathExpressions: \text{C: smallest abstraction over machine} \implies \text{universal ABI, slow to die}
